title: Milestone: Stories That Last
objective: After this level you can connect myths, storytelling craft and the old classics to explain why some stories survive for centuries.
summary: Why stories last: a single copy survives by luck (Nineveh, Beowulf), a great poem carries a language (Ferdowsi, Dante, Chaucer), and new ages retell and translate them.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway. Why do some stories outlive the empires that made them?
cards.body: You've traveled from clay tablets to the road to Canterbury. Some stories survived by a thread, some carried a whole language, and some keep being retold. Here's the pattern.

cards.headline: Kept: one copy can be enough
cards.body: Remember Level 10: stories survive by memory, copying and luck. Luck kept Ashurbanipal's tablets, buried under Nineveh's walls when the city was sacked in 612 BCE. Luck again kept Beowulf: its single manuscript, made around the year 1000, came through a fire in 1731 with much of its text still readable. Sometimes a whole literature rests on one survivor.

cards.headline: Carried: a language in a book

items.label: Shahnameh (1010)
points: Pure Persian, with only a trace of Arabic

items.label: Divine Comedy (1308 to 1321)
points: Italian instead of Latin, for a wider audience

items.label: Canterbury Tales (1387 to 1400)
points: English, while Gower also wrote in French and Latin

cards.headline: Retold and translated
cards.body: Stories also last when new ages retell them. Antigone's clash of law and conscience returned in occupied Paris in 1944. Ovid gave poets and painters of the 15th to 17th centuries their myths. The Nights kept growing when Hanna Diyab told Galland stories in 1709. And translation carries a story across languages: English readers got The Tale of Genji, often called the first novel, from Arthur Waley between 1925 and 1933.

mascot.line: Keep this: a story lasts when a copy survives, when it carries a language, and when new ages retell and translate it.

cards.headline: Milestone: stories that last
learned: How stories survived by performance, from Homer's singers to Mali's griots, and by lucky copies like Beowulf.
Why myths from Scandinavia to India, Africa and the Americas rhyme, and how they traveled with their tellers.
How to take a story apart into plot, conflict, characters, narrator and theme.
How meter, sound, imagery and form make a poem, and what epics and tragedies are built from.
Why Ferdowsi, Dante and Chaucer wrote in their people's language, and how retelling keeps old stories alive.

questions.prompt: What do Ashurbanipal's tablets from Nineveh and the Beowulf manuscript show about how old stories survive?

options.label: Rulers had every great poem copied many times
options.rationale: Ashurbanipal's scribes copied texts, but Beowulf has only one manuscript.

options.label: Scholars rewrote lost poems from memory
options.rationale: Nothing was rewritten: the old tablets and the manuscript themselves came through.

options.label: Sometimes one lucky survivor keeps a whole work
Clay and parchment never decay or burn
options.rationale: Nineveh was sacked and Beowulf's manuscript was damaged by fire in 1731.

questions.explanation: Nineveh's ruined walls buried its tablets in 612 BCE, and Beowulf's single manuscript came through a fire in 1731. Luck decided what we can still read.

questions.prompt: How has the epic of Sundiata been kept alive in West Africa for centuries?

options.label: Griots, hereditary storytellers, keep performing it
Monks copied it into one illuminated manuscript
options.rationale: That's closer to how Beowulf survived.

options.label: Mali's scribes pressed it into clay tablets
options.rationale: Clay tablets carried Gilgamesh, not Sundiata.

options.label: It stayed secret until a printed book in 1960
options.rationale: Niane's 1960 book is presented as a griot's telling, not a first discovery.

questions.explanation: Griots (jeli) are hereditary troubadour-historians who preserve genealogies and histories by performing them, many playing the kora. Even on paper, a griot does the talking.

questions.prompt: What do the Shahnameh, the Divine Comedy and the Canterbury Tales have in common?

options.label: Each is a frame story of unfinished tales
options.rationale: Only Chaucer's uses a storytelling frame.

options.label: Each was written in Latin for scholars
options.rationale: None of them was.

options.label: Each survives in a single manuscript
options.rationale: That's Beowulf.

options.label: Each gave its own people's language a great poem

questions.explanation: Ferdowsi wrote in pure Persian, Dante in Italian instead of Latin, and Chaucer in English: each raised a language with a great poem.

questions.prompt: Level 26 turned a subject into a theme. Which of these states a theme of Sophocles' Antigone, not just its subject or plot?

options.label: Law against conscience in ancient Thebes
options.rationale: That's a subject: a topic with no assertion about it.

options.label: A ruler who puts his law above all can lose everything
Antigone buries her brother against Creon's order
options.rationale: That's what happens: a plot summary.

options.label: Citizens must always obey their city's laws
options.rationale: That's a moral, and a theme need not be one; the play doesn't teach it either.

questions.explanation: A theme adds an assertion to a subject, in one sentence. Creon holds to his edict so rigidly that he loses his son and his wife and is left alone with his law.

questions.prompt: Homer's Iliad opens "Sing, O goddess"; Milton opened Paradise Lost with "Sing, Heavenly Muse", keeping the epic convention of _____.

options.label: in medias res
options.rationale: That's plunging into the middle of the story, a different opening habit.

options.label: the epic simile
options.rationale: That's a comparison stretched over several lines.

options.label: the type-scene
options.rationale: That's a recurring story block, like arming or a feast, from Level 6.

options.label: the invocation

questions.explanation: Calling on a Muse or god for inspiration is the invocation. Homer's epics open with it, and Milton kept the habit: a convention that outlasted the singers who made it.

questions.prompt: Anouilh retold Antigone in 1944. Which Chapter 1 work lasted the same way, as later poets and painters borrowed from it?

options.label: The Kojiki
options.rationale: It survived by being written down from memory.

options.label: Ovid's Metamorphoses
The Enuma Elish
options.rationale: It was recited at the Babylonian New Year festival.

options.label: The Epic of Gilgamesh
options.rationale: It survived on buried clay tablets.

questions.explanation: From the 15th to 17th centuries, it's hard to name a poet or painter of note who didn't owe something to Ovid.

questions.prompt: The Nights kept growing as its tales traveled, from Aleppo to Paris. Which story from Chapter 2 also spread with its tellers into new local forms?

options.label: The Popol Vuh
options.rationale: Its original is lost; one copy from the early 1700s survives.

options.label: The Poetic Edda
options.rationale: It was copied down in Iceland in the 13th century.

options.label: The Ramayana
The Icelandic sagas
options.rationale: They tell of Iceland's own farming families.

questions.explanation: Stories travel with the people who tell them. The Ramayana spread through Southeast Asia: Thailand's Ramakien is the basis of khon dance-drama.
